sets.title: Coded Direction-Distance Network
sets.context:
Distance and direction between points is coded as follows:
'A # B' means A is west of B.
'A & B' means A is south of B.
'A @ B' means A is north of B.
'A % B' means A is east of B.
'N * AB' means N is the midpoint of line AB.
A network of points is linked as: L @ Z, S # K, R % H, Q # Z, T # M, Q & H, S & M, T @ R (so R, H, T and M are all linked into one cluster via H and R, and via T and M).

sets.title: Eight Persons - City, Weight and Code Puzzle
sets.context:
Eight persons A, B, C, D, E, F, G and H live in eight different cities - Chennai, Bangalore, Hyderabad, Mumbai, Ahmedabad, Ernakulam, Jaipur and Bhubaneshwar - and each has a different weight from 89, 50, 55, 71, 49, 66, 92 and 56 kg.
A has a weight which is a multiple of both 11 and 5, and lives in Bhubaneshwar. D lives in Bangalore, but his weight is not 89 kg or 71 kg. The one who lives in Hyderabad has a weight of 56 kg. G has a weight of 49 kg and does not live in Mumbai or Chennai. E has a weight of 71 kg and lives in Ahmedabad or Ernakulam. F lives in Chennai but his weight is not 92 kg. C lives in Mumbai. The sum of the weights of H and C is 181 kg. Neither G nor H lives in Ernakulam. G does not live in Jaipur. The sum of the weights of D and H is 142 kg.
A code is further assigned to each person based on the first letter of their city and their weight:
1. If the city starts with a vowel and the weight is prime, the code is the 5th succeeding letter of the person's own name (as per the English alphabet).
2. If the city starts with a vowel and the weight is composite, the code is the 3rd preceding letter of the person's own name.
3. If the city starts with a consonant and the weight is prime, the code is the sum of the digits of the person's weight.
4. If the city starts with a consonant and the weight is composite, the code is the difference of the digits of the person's weight.

sets.title: Actual Work vs Maximum Time Table
sets.context:
Three persons A, B and C have the following actual work done (in units) and maximum time (in hours) to complete that work at their respective minimum efficiency:

| Person | Actual work done | Maximum time (hrs) |
|---|---|---|
| A | 50 units | 10 |
| B | 60 units | 12 |
| C | - | 15 |

Each person's minimum efficiency (units/hr) equals their actual work divided by their maximum time (so A's and B's minimum efficiency = 5 units/hr each). When a person works at a boosted efficiency, they finish their fixed actual work faster than their maximum time, and the leftover time within that maximum-time window counts as rest.

Conclusions:
I. T W L

questions.question:
Six people - Megha, Suhas, Rakesh, Akshay, Safia and Nidhi - are standing in a line according to their height, but not necessarily in that order. Who is the second tallest person?
Statement I: Megha is taller than just two persons. Rakesh is taller than Nidhi and Safia but he is not the tallest. Suhas is shorter than just two persons.
Statement II: Nidhi is the second shortest person. Megha is shorter than three persons. Suhas is shorter than Akshay and Rakesh. Safia is the shortest.
options: The data in statement I alone is sufficient to answer the question, while the data in statement II alone is not sufficient to answer the question
The data in statement II alone is sufficient to answer the question, while the data in statement I alone is not sufficient to answer the question
The data either in statement I alone or in statement II alone is sufficient to answer the question
The data in both statements I and II together is not sufficient to answer the question
The data in both statements I and II together is necessary to answer the question
questions.explanation: Statement I alone: Megha is 4th tallest, Suhas is 3rd tallest; since Rakesh (taller than Nidhi and Safia, but not tallest) must then be 2nd tallest with Akshay 1st and Nidhi/Safia last - Rakesh is uniquely the 2nd tallest. Statement II alone: it fixes Safia=6th, Nidhi=5th, Megha=4th, Suhas=3rd, but leaves Akshay and Rakesh interchangeable between 1st and 2nd - not sufficient alone.

questions.question:
Which of the following statements is sufficient to find the shortest distance between points M and J?
I. J & P, P % N, N @ O
II. P & Q, N % P, O @ N, O # J
options: Data in Statement I alone is sufficient, while Statement II alone is not sufficient
Data in Statement II alone is sufficient, while Statement I alone is not sufficient
Data either in Statement I alone or Statement II alone is sufficient
Data in both statements together is not sufficient
Data in both statements together is necessary
questions.explanation: M is already linked to the fixed network through T and R/H (T # M, T @ R, R % H, Q & H). Statement I only strings J-P-N-O together in an isolated cluster with no link back to the M/T/R/H network, so it cannot fix the M-J distance. Statement II's P & Q line bridges P (and hence its N-O-J chain) to Q, which is already part of the fixed network, giving one continuous path from M through T/R/H/Q/P/N/O to J - so Statement II alone is sufficient.

questions.question:
Conclusions:
I. All Roots can not be Grass.
II. Some Leaves being Grass is a possibility.
Statements:
I. Some Roots are Grass. All Trees are Leaves. Some Leaves are Roots.
II. Only a few Leaves are Roots. Some Roots are Grass. All Trees are Leaves.
III. Only a few Leaves are Roots. Some Roots are Grass. Some Trees are Leaves.
IV. Only a few Roots are Grass. All Trees are Leaves. Some Leaves are Roots.
V. Only a few Roots are Grass. Some Trees are Leaves. Some Leaves are Roots.

Testing each statement's Venn diagram, both statement IV and statement V (each built on 'Only a few Roots are Grass' rather than 'Some Roots are Grass') leave room for a diagram where Roots and Grass are entirely separate while still allowing a Leaves-Grass overlap, so both conclusions hold as possibilities under either IV or V.

I. At least some goat being bird is a possibility.
II. Some swans are goat.
Statements:
I. All goats are Swans. All swans are crows. No goat is a bird.

III. Some goats are Swans. Some goats are crows. No goat is a bird.

Statement V says 'No crow is a bird' rather than 'no goat is a bird', so goats (all of whom are swans, hence crows) being birds is only excluded if crows can't be birds - but since 'No crow is a bird' is given and all goats are crows, goats also cannot be birds definitively, which nonetheless leaves the 'possibility' wording of conclusion I intact by the book's convention.
